1.1.title: The poet invokes the Muse
1.1.text: The poet asks the Muse to tell of the man who wandered long after the sack of Troy and could not save his comrades. The other survivors of the war are home, but the nymph Calypso keeps Odysseus in her caves and wants him for her husband. Now the year has come in which the gods have decided he shall return to Ithaca. All the gods pity him except Poseidon.

1.2.title: The gods meet on Olympus
1.2.text: Poseidon is away among the Ethiopians, and the other gods meet in the halls of Zeus on Olympus. Athena pleads for Odysseus, held on Calypso's island. Zeus agrees that he must come home, though Poseidon is angry with him for blinding his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus. Athena asks that Hermes be sent to Ogygia; she herself will go to Ithaca, rouse Odysseus' son and send him to Sparta and Pylos for news.

1.3.title: Athena comes to Ithaca
1.3.text: Athena takes her spear and darts down from Olympus to Ithaca. She stands at the gate of Odysseus' palace in the shape of Mentes, lord of the Taphians, while the suitors play draughts in front of the doors. Telemachus is the first to see the stranger; he welcomes him, seats him apart from the suitors and has food brought. The suitors come in to feast, and afterwards the bard Phemius takes up his lyre.

1.4.title: The stranger from Taphos
1.4.text: Telemachus leans close to his guest so that the suitors cannot hear, and asks who he is. Athena answers as Mentes, lord of the Taphians and an old friend of the house, who is sailing to Temesa to trade iron for copper. She has heard that Laertes no longer comes to town and lives out on his farm. She says that Odysseus is not dead but held on an island in the open sea, and foretells that he will soon find his way home.

1.5.title: Telemachus tells of the suitors
1.5.text: Athena asks what feast this is, for the guests behave like men without shame. Telemachus answers that the house was rich once, but his father has vanished without a trace. Now the lords of Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus, and those of Ithaca itself, all court his mother and eat up his house. Penelope neither refuses to marry nor can put an end to it.

1.6.title: Athena's advice
1.6.text: Athena wishes Odysseus stood at the door in arms, as strong as when he once came back from Ephyra. She tells Telemachus to call an assembly tomorrow and order the suitors to go home. Then he must take a ship with twenty rowers and ask Nestor in Pylos and Menelaus in Sparta for news of his father. She leaves like a bird in flight, and Telemachus understands that his guest was a god.

1.7.title: Penelope and Phemius' song
1.7.text: Phemius sings of the hard return of the Achaeans from Troy, and the suitors listen in silence. Penelope hears the song from her upper room, comes down with two maids and in tears asks him to sing something else. Telemachus tells his mother not to blame the bard and sends her back to her loom, saying that he is master in the house. Amazed, she goes upstairs and weeps for Odysseus until Athena sends her sleep.

1.8.title: Telemachus defies the suitors
1.8.text: Telemachus tells the suitors that in the morning he will call them to the assembly and order them out of his house. They bite their lips, surprised at how boldly he speaks. Antinous hopes that Zeus will never make him king of Ithaca, and Eurymachus asks who the stranger was. Telemachus answers that it was Mentes of Taphos, a friend of his father, though in his heart he knows it was a goddess.

1.9.title: Telemachus goes to bed
1.9.text: The suitors dance and sing until dark and then go home to sleep. Telemachus goes to his bedroom off the courtyard, and the old servant Eurycleia lights his way with torches. Laertes bought her long ago for the price of twenty oxen, and she nursed Telemachus when he was a child. All night he lies under a fleece and thinks about the journey that Athena has shown him.

2.1.title: Telemachus calls the assembly
2.1.text: At dawn Telemachus has the heralds call the Achaeans to the assembly place and sits down in his father's seat. Old Aegyptius asks who has summoned them, for they have not met since Odysseus sailed away. Telemachus takes the speaker's staff and accuses the suitors of crowding his house and eating up his goods day after day. He throws the staff to the ground in tears, and the people pity him.

2.2.title: Antinous blames Penelope
2.2.text: Antinous answers that Penelope herself is to blame. For three years she put the suitors off: by day she wove a shroud for Laertes and by night she unpicked it, until one of her maids gave her away. He demands that Telemachus send his mother back to her father Icarius to be married. Telemachus refuses to drive her from the house and calls on Zeus to punish the suitors.

2.3.title: Two eagles over the assembly
2.3.text: Zeus sends two eagles, which wheel over the assembly, tear at each other with their talons and fly off over the town. The old seer Halitherses says the sign means that Odysseus is near and is planning death for the suitors. He recalls his own prophecy that Odysseus would come home in the twentieth year, alone and unrecognised. Eurymachus mocks the seer, threatens him with a fine and says the suitors fear no one.

2.4.title: The assembly breaks up
2.4.text: Telemachus asks for a fast ship and twenty men, so that he can sail to Sparta and Pylos for news of his father. Mentor, to whom Odysseus entrusted his household, scolds the people for sitting silent while a few suitors ruin it. Leocritus answers that even Odysseus would die if he fought so many men, and he dissolves the assembly. The people go home, and the suitors go back to the palace of Odysseus.

2.5.title: Athena comes as Mentor
2.5.text: Telemachus walks alone to the seashore, washes his hands in the grey water and prays to Athena. She comes to him in the shape and voice of Mentor and tells him that his journey will not be in vain. She promises to find a fast ship and a crew and to sail with him herself. He is to go home and pack wine in jars and barley meal in leather bags.

2.6.title: The suitors mock Telemachus
2.6.text: Telemachus comes home and finds the suitors skinning goats and singeing pigs in the courtyard. Antinous laughs, takes his hand and invites him to eat and drink with them as before. Telemachus pulls his hand away and says he will go to Pylos, even as a passenger on another man's ship. The suitors jeer that he will fetch fighters from Pylos or Sparta or poison from Ephyra, or will be lost at sea like Odysseus.

2.7.title: Eurycleia in the storeroom
2.7.text: Telemachus goes down to his father's storeroom, which the old nurse Eurycleia guards day and night. He asks her for twelve jars of wine and twenty measures of barley meal and tells her that he is sailing to Sparta and Pylos. She cries out and begs him to stay, because the suitors will plot his death as soon as he is gone. He makes her swear to say nothing to his mother for eleven or twelve days.

2.8.title: The ship sails at night
2.8.text: Athena takes the shape of Telemachus, gathers a crew in the town and borrows a ship from Noemon. After sunset she pours sleep over the suitors, and they go off to their beds in the town. Then, as Mentor, she leads Telemachus down to the harbour, where the men load the stores and cast off. Athena sends a west wind, and the ship runs all night and into the dawn.

3.1.title: Landing at Pylos
3.1.text: At sunrise the ship reaches Pylos, where the people are sacrificing black bulls to Poseidon on the shore. Athena, still in the shape of Mentor, tells Telemachus not to be shy and to go straight to Nestor. Nestor's son Peisistratus takes the two strangers by the hand and seats them on fleeces on the sand. Athena and then Telemachus pour wine and pray to Poseidon, and everyone shares the feast.

3.2.title: Telemachus asks about his father
3.2.text: After the meal Nestor asks the strangers who they are. Telemachus says that he has come from Ithaca to seek news of his father Odysseus, and begs Nestor to tell him the truth. Nestor remembers the long war at Troy, where Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus and his own son Antilochus lie dead. He says that no one there could match Odysseus in cunning and that the two of them never disagreed in council.

3.3.title: Nestor's voyage home
3.3.text: Nestor tells how the Achaeans quarrelled after taking Troy and half the army sailed without Agamemnon. At Tenedos Odysseus turned back to him, but Nestor and Diomedes fled on to Lesbos, where Menelaus caught up with them. They did not know whether to pass outside Chios, by Psyria, or inside it past Mimas, until a god's sign sent them straight across the open sea to Geraestus on Euboea. Diomedes landed at Argos, and Nestor sailed on to Pylos.

3.4.title: Athena rebukes Telemachus
3.4.text: Nestor has heard that Achilles' son, Philoctetes and Idomeneus came home safe, and that Agamemnon was murdered by Aegisthus and avenged by his son. Telemachus wishes he had such strength against the suitors, but says he cannot hope for it, even if the gods willed it. Athena, as Mentor, rebukes him: a god can easily bring a man home safe, even from far away. Telemachus then asks how Agamemnon died and where Menelaus was.

3.5.title: Nestor's tale of Menelaus
3.5.text: Nestor tells how Aegisthus seduced Clytemnestra, murdered Agamemnon and ruled Mycenae for seven years, until Orestes killed him. Menelaus was far away: he had stopped at Cape Sunium to bury his helmsman, and at Cape Malea a storm scattered his ships. Some were wrecked on Crete near Phaestus, and five were driven to Egypt. Nestor advises Telemachus to visit Menelaus in Sparta and offers him a chariot and his sons as guides.

3.6.title: Nestor invites Telemachus home
3.6.text: The sun sets, and at Athena's word they throw the victims' tongues on the fire and pour a libation to Poseidon. Athena and Telemachus turn to go back to the ship, but Nestor will not let the son of Odysseus sleep on a ship's deck. Athena agrees that Telemachus should sleep in Nestor's house, while she spends the night by the ship with the crew. She asks Nestor to send Telemachus on by chariot with one of his sons.

3.7.title: Nestor recognises Athena
3.7.text: Athena flies away in the shape of a sea-eagle, and everyone is amazed. Nestor takes Telemachus by the hand and tells him that his companion was Athena herself; he vows to sacrifice to her a heifer with gilded horns. He leads his sons and his guest to his palace, where they pour old wine to the goddess. Telemachus sleeps in the portico, with Peisistratus beside him.

3.8.title: The sacrifice to Athena
3.8.text: At dawn Nestor sits on the white stones before his doors and sends for a heifer, a goldsmith and Telemachus' crew. The smith gilds the heifer's horns; Thrasymedes fells her with an axe, Peisistratus cuts her throat, and Nestor burns the thigh pieces for Athena. Polycaste, Nestor's youngest daughter, bathes Telemachus and dresses him in a fine cloak and tunic. Then they all sit down to the feast.

3.9.title: By chariot to Pherae
3.9.text: Nestor has horses yoked for Telemachus, and the housekeeper puts bread, wine and other food in the chariot. Peisistratus takes the reins, and the two leave Pylos and drive all day. At sunset they reach Pherae and spend the night as guests in the house of Diocles. At dawn they drive on through a plain of wheat and press towards the end of their road until the sun sets again.

4.1.title: Arrival at Sparta
4.1.text: Telemachus and Peisistratus reach Sparta, where Menelaus is holding a wedding feast for his son Megapenthes and his daughter Hermione. Menelaus has the strangers brought in, bathed and seated beside him. He tells how he wandered by Cyprus, Phoenicia, Egypt and Libya, gathered great wealth and came home in the eighth year. Of all his lost comrades he mourns Odysseus most, he says, and Telemachus hides his tears behind his cloak.

4.2.title: Helen recognises Telemachus
4.2.text: Helen comes out of her chamber, and her maids bring her chair and her silver wool basket. She says at once that the young guest looks just like Telemachus, the son of Odysseus, and Peisistratus confirms that it is he. Menelaus speaks of his love for Odysseus, and all four weep; Peisistratus thinks of his brother Antilochus, who died at Troy. At Peisistratus' request they stop weeping and go back to their supper.

4.3.title: Tales of Odysseus at Troy
4.3.text: Helen slips into the wine a drug from Egypt that takes away all grief. She tells how Odysseus once stole into Troy disguised as a beggar; she alone knew him and kept his secret. Menelaus tells how the heroes sat hidden in the wooden horse while Helen walked round it calling their names in their wives' voices, and Odysseus kept them silent. Then Helen has beds made in the portico for the two guests.

4.4.title: Telemachus asks Menelaus
4.4.text: At dawn Menelaus asks Telemachus what has brought him to Sparta. Telemachus says that suitors are eating up his house, and begs to hear the truth about his father. Menelaus angrily says that Odysseus will fall on them like a lion on fawns left in its lair, and wishes him back as strong as when he threw Philomeleides in wrestling on Lesbos. He promises to hide nothing of what the Old Man of the Sea told him.

4.5.title: Menelaus catches Proteus
4.5.text: Menelaus tells how the gods held him for twenty windless days on Pharos, an island off Egypt. The goddess Eidothea pitied him and hid him with three of his men under sealskins among the seals of her father Proteus. At noon Proteus lay down among them, and they held him fast while he changed shape: lion, snake, leopard, boar, water, tree. At last he told Menelaus to sail back to the river Aigyptos and sacrifice to the gods before going home.

4.6.title: Proteus' news
4.6.text: Menelaus tells what else Proteus said: Ajax son of Oileus drowned at the Gyraean Rocks, and Aegisthus killed Agamemnon at a feast. A third chief was alive: Odysseus sat in tears on the island of Calypso, who kept him there without ship or crew. For Menelaus himself Proteus foretold the Elysian plain at the ends of the earth. Menelaus sailed back to the river Aigyptos, sacrificed, raised a mound for Agamemnon and had a fair wind home.

4.7.title: A gift for Telemachus
4.7.text: Menelaus invites Telemachus to stay eleven or twelve days and offers him three horses and a chariot. Telemachus answers that his crew is waiting at Pylos and that Ithaca has no room for horses, only pasture for goats. Menelaus smiles and promises him instead a silver mixing bowl with a golden rim, a gift from the king of the Sidonians. The guests arrive at the palace with sheep and wine for the day's feast.

4.8.title: The suitors plan an ambush
4.8.text: In front of the palace of Odysseus the suitors are throwing the discus and the javelin. Noemon asks Antinous when Telemachus will be back from Pylos: he lent him his ship and now needs it to cross to Elis. The suitors are astonished, for they thought Telemachus was somewhere on his farms. Antinous asks for a fast ship and twenty men to lie in wait for him in the strait between Ithaca and Same.

4.9.title: Penelope learns of the plot
4.9.text: The herald Medon has overheard the suitors and tells Penelope that they mean to kill Telemachus on his way home. Her knees give way; she sinks down on the threshold of her room and laments that no one told her he had gone. Eurycleia admits that she knew and was sworn to silence, and advises her to pray to Athena and not to trouble old Laertes. Penelope washes, goes upstairs and prays to the goddess to save her son.

4.10.title: The ambush and the dream
4.10.text: Antinous picks twenty men; they launch a ship, moor her a little way out and wait for evening. Penelope lies upstairs without food or drink until she falls asleep. Athena sends her a phantom in the shape of her sister Iphthime: it says that Telemachus will come home, since Athena travels with him, but will not speak of Odysseus. The suitors sail to the rocky islet of Asteris, between Ithaca and Same, and lie in wait there.

5.1.title: The gods in council
5.1.text: At dawn the gods sit in council on Olympus. Athena reminds them that the nymph Calypso holds Odysseus on her island without ship or crew, and that the suitors plan to kill Telemachus on his way back from Pylos and Sparta. Zeus tells her to bring Telemachus home safely. He sends Hermes to Calypso with his decision: Odysseus is to leave on a raft and reach Scheria, the land of the Phaeacians, who will send him home by ship.

5.2.title: Hermes flies to Ogygia
5.2.text: Hermes puts on his golden sandals, takes his wand and flies down from Olympus. He touches Pieria and then skims over the waves like a seabird until he reaches the far island of Ogygia. In a great cave among trees, vines and four springs he finds Calypso singing at her loom. Odysseus is not there: he sits on the shore, weeping and looking out over the sea.

5.3.title: Hermes brings Zeus' order
5.3.text: Calypso seats Hermes, asks why he has come and serves him ambrosia and nectar. Hermes says that Zeus orders her to send Odysseus away at once, because it is his fate to see his home again. Calypso complains that the gods grudge a goddess a mortal husband; she saved Odysseus when Zeus wrecked his ship, she says, and offered to make him immortal. She gives in and promises him her advice, and Hermes leaves.

5.4.title: Calypso lets Odysseus go
5.4.text: Calypso finds Odysseus weeping on the shore and tells him to build a raft, because she will let him go. Odysseus suspects a trap, and she swears by earth, heaven and the Styx that she plans him no harm. In the cave, after supper, she says that many troubles await him and that with her he could be immortal. Odysseus answers that Penelope cannot compare with a goddess, yet he longs for home and will bear whatever comes.

5.5.title: By raft from Ogygia
5.5.text: At dawn Calypso gives Odysseus an axe and an adze and shows him where the tall trees grow. He fells twenty trees and in four days builds a raft with a mast, a sail and a steering oar. On the fifth day Calypso gives him food, water and wine and sends a warm following wind. Odysseus sails for seventeen days, keeping the Bear on his left, and on the eighteenth the mountains of the Phaeacians' land come into sight.

5.6.title: Poseidon raises a storm
5.6.text: On his way back from the Ethiopians, Poseidon sees the raft from the far-off mountains of the Solymi and is angry that Odysseus is so near the land of the Phaeacians. He gathers the clouds, stirs up the sea with his trident and lets loose all the winds at once. Odysseus wishes he had died at Troy and been buried with honour. A great wave throws him off the raft and the gale snaps the mast, but he struggles back on board.

5.7.title: Ino's veil
5.7.text: Ino Leucothea, once a mortal and now a sea goddess, pities Odysseus, rises from the water and sits on the raft. She gives him her veil and tells him to strip, leave the raft and swim for the land of the Phaeacians. Odysseus fears a trick and stays aboard until a great wave sent by Poseidon scatters the timbers. Then he ties the veil under his chest and dives into the sea, and Poseidon drives his horses off to his palace at Aegae.

5.8.title: Two days in the waves
5.8.text: Athena stills the other winds and sends a north wind to carry Odysseus towards the Phaeacians. For two days and two nights he drifts on the swell, and on the third day he sees land close by. The shore is all cliffs and reefs, with no harbour. A wave throws him against a rock; he clings to it, is dragged back out to sea with the skin torn from his hands, and swims along the coast looking for a place to land.

5.9.title: Ashore at the river mouth
5.9.text: Odysseus reaches the mouth of a river and prays to the river god for mercy. The god holds back his current and lets him come ashore, exhausted and swollen from the sea. Odysseus throws Ino's veil back into the water and kisses the earth. Fearing the cold by the river, he goes up to a wood, creeps under two close-grown bushes and covers himself with leaves, and Athena sends him sleep.

6.1.title: Athena in Nausicaa's dream
6.1.text: While Odysseus sleeps, Athena goes to the city of the Phaeacians on Scheria. The Phaeacians once lived near the Cyclopes, who raided them, until Nausithous led them here; now Alcinous is their king. Athena comes to the bedside of his daughter Nausicaa in the form of a friend of her own age. She tells her to take the clothes to the washing place at dawn, because her wedding is near, and then returns to Olympus.

6.2.title: Nausicaa asks for a wagon
6.2.text: At dawn Nausicaa wakes, wonders at her dream and goes to look for her parents. Her mother is spinning by the hearth, and her father Alcinous is on his way to the council. Nausicaa asks him for a wagon to take the family's clothes to the river; she is too shy to speak of her own wedding, but he understands. The mules are yoked, her mother packs food, wine and oil, and Nausicaa drives off with her maids.

6.3.title: Washing day at the river
6.3.text: Nausicaa and her maids reach the washing place at the river. They wash the clothes, spread them on the shore to dry, bathe, eat and then play ball. When it is time to go home, Athena sees to it that Nausicaa's throw misses and the ball falls into the river. The girls cry out, and Odysseus wakes and wonders what kind of people live in this land.

6.4.title: Odysseus meets Nausicaa
6.4.text: Odysseus comes out of the bushes, naked behind a leafy branch, and all the girls run away except Nausicaa. From a distance he praises her, likening her to a young palm tree he once saw on Delos. He says the sea has carried him for twenty days from Ogygia, and asks for clothing and the way to the city. Nausicaa promises help and tells him that this is the land of the Phaeacians and that she is the daughter of King Alcinous.

6.5.title: A bath and clean clothes
6.5.text: Nausicaa calls her maids back and tells them to give the stranger food, drink and a bath in the river. Odysseus asks the girls to stand aside, washes off the brine, rubs himself with oil and puts on the clothes they have left for him. Athena makes him taller and more handsome. Nausicaa tells her maids that she would like such a man for a husband, and Odysseus eats and drinks hungrily.

6.6.title: Nausicaa's advice
6.6.text: Nausicaa loads the clothes, yokes the mules and tells Odysseus what to do. He is to follow the wagon with the maids through the fields, but wait in the grove of Athena near the city, so that no one sees them together and gossips. Then he is to ask for the palace of Alcinous, go straight through the hall and clasp the knees of her mother by the hearth. If the queen is kind to him, she says, he may hope to see his home.

6.7.title: In the grove of Athena
6.7.text: Nausicaa drives the mules at a pace that lets Odysseus and the maids keep up on foot. At sunset they reach the grove of Athena, and Odysseus sits down there. He prays to Athena that the Phaeacians may receive him with kindness and pity. Athena hears him but does not show herself, out of respect for her uncle Poseidon, who is still angry with Odysseus.

7.1.title: Odysseus enters the city
7.1.text: Nausicaa reaches her father's palace and goes to her room. Odysseus leaves the grove for the city, and Athena wraps him in a thick mist so that no Phaeacian will stop him and ask who he is. At the edge of the city she meets him in the form of a girl with a pitcher and leads him to the palace of Alcinous. On the way Odysseus admires the harbours, the ships and the long, high walls.

7.2.title: Athena speaks of Arete
7.2.text: At the door of the palace Athena tells Odysseus to go in without fear and to approach Queen Arete first. She tells him that Arete is the daughter of Rhexenor, the king's dead brother, and that their father Nausithous was a son of Poseidon. Alcinous married her, and he, her children and the whole people honour her. If Arete is kind to him, Athena says, he may hope to see his home again.

7.3.title: The palace and the garden
7.3.text: Athena leaves Scheria and crosses the sea to Marathon and Athens. Odysseus stops in front of the palace of Alcinous: its walls are of bronze and its doors of gold, and gold and silver dogs made by Hephaestus guard the entrance. Next to the courtyard lies a large orchard with a vineyard and two springs, where pears, pomegranates, apples, figs and olives ripen all year round. Odysseus stands and looks at it all.

7.4.title: Odysseus clasps Arete's knees
7.4.text: Odysseus enters the hall, where the Phaeacian leaders are pouring a last libation to Hermes before bed. Hidden in the mist, he walks up to Arete and clasps her knees; the mist lifts and everyone falls silent. He asks to be sent home and sits down in the ashes by the hearth. Old Echeneus reminds Alcinous how a guest should be treated, and the king raises Odysseus, seats him in the chair of his son Laodamas and has food and wine brought.

7.5.title: Alcinous promises help
7.5.text: Alcinous tells the leaders to go home and come back in the morning: they will feast the stranger, sacrifice to the gods and then see to his journey home. He wonders aloud whether the stranger may be a god. Odysseus answers that he is a mortal who has suffered more than most, and asks only to finish his supper and to be taken home at dawn. The Phaeacians approve his words.

7.6.title: Odysseus answers Arete
7.6.text: The guests go home, and Odysseus stays in the hall with Arete and Alcinous. Arete recognises the clothes he is wearing and asks who he is and who gave them to him. Odysseus tells how Zeus wrecked his ship and he drifted to Ogygia, where Calypso kept him for seven years, and how he left on a raft that Poseidon's storm broke up. He says that he swam to the river mouth, and that Nausicaa gave him food and these clothes.

7.7.title: A bed in the portico
7.7.text: Alcinous says that his daughter should have brought the stranger home herself; Odysseus answers that he chose to stay behind. Alcinous would like such a man to stay and marry his daughter, but promises not to keep him against his will. He sets the voyage for the next day and says that his rowers will carry Odysseus home in his sleep, however far it is. Arete has a bed made in the portico, and Odysseus lies down there.

8.1.title: The assembly of the Phaeacians
8.1.text: At dawn Alcinous leads Odysseus to the assembly place beside the ships. Athena, in the form of the king's herald, calls the Phaeacians together and makes Odysseus taller and more imposing. Alcinous has a new ship launched and fifty-two young rowers chosen to take the stranger home. He invites the leaders and the rowers to a feast in the palace and sends for the bard Demodocus.

8.2.title: Demodocus' first song
8.2.text: The herald leads the blind bard Demodocus into the hall and seats him among the guests. After the meal Demodocus sings how Odysseus and Achilles quarrel at a feast and Agamemnon is glad of it, because Apollo foretold this to him at Pytho when the troubles of Trojans and Achaeans were beginning. Odysseus pulls his cloak over his head to hide his tears. Only Alcinous notices, and he proposes that they go out and hold games.

8.3.title: The Phaeacian games
8.3.text: The Phaeacians go to the assembly place for the games. The young men compete in running, wrestling, jumping, discus and boxing; Euryalus wins the wrestling and Laodamas, the king's son, the boxing. Laodamas invites the stranger to compete, and Odysseus answers that his mind is on his troubles and his journey home. Euryalus then mocks him to his face: he looks like a trader who thinks only of cargo and profit, not like an athlete.

8.4.title: Odysseus throws the discus
8.4.text: Odysseus answers Euryalus angrily that he is handsome but speaks without sense. Still in his cloak, he picks up a discus heavier than the ones the Phaeacians use and throws it far beyond all their marks. Athena, in the form of a man, marks the spot and says that no one will beat it. Odysseus then challenges any Phaeacian except his host Laodamas to box, wrestle or race, and says that at Troy only Philoctetes was a better archer.

8.5.title: Alcinous calls the dancers
8.5.text: After a silence only Alcinous answers. He says that the Phaeacians are no great boxers or wrestlers, but fast runners and the best seamen, and that they love feasts, the lyre, dancing, fresh clothes, warm baths and their beds. He calls for the best dancers and has the lyre fetched for Demodocus. A dancing floor is levelled, the young men dance around the bard, and Odysseus watches their quick feet.

8.6.title: Song of Ares and Aphrodite
8.6.text: Demodocus sings of Ares and Aphrodite, who lie together in secret in the house of Hephaestus. Warned by Helios, Hephaestus forges chains as fine as cobwebs, hangs them over the bed and pretends to leave for Lemnos. The chains catch the lovers, and Hephaestus calls the gods, who laugh at the sight. Poseidon stands surety for the fine Ares owes; set free, Ares goes to Thrace and Aphrodite to Paphos on Cyprus.

8.7.title: Gifts and an apology
8.7.text: Alcinous has his sons Halius and Laodamas dance alone with a purple ball, and Odysseus praises the dancers. Pleased, the king proposes guest-gifts: each of the twelve kings is to bring a cloak, a tunic and a talent of gold, and Euryalus must make amends. Euryalus gives Odysseus a bronze sword with a silver hilt and an ivory scabbard and asks him to forget the insult. Odysseus wishes him well and slings the sword over his shoulder.

8.8.title: Nausicaa says farewell
8.8.text: At sunset the gifts are carried to the palace. Alcinous adds a golden cup, and Arete packs everything in a chest with a cloak and a tunic; Odysseus ties the lid with a knot that Circe once taught him. The maids bathe him in warm water. On his way to the feast Nausicaa asks him to remember her at home, since he owes her his life, and Odysseus answers that, if he gets home, he will pray to her there as to a goddess.

8.9.title: Song of the wooden horse
8.9.text: At the feast Odysseus sends Demodocus a portion of meat and asks for the song of the wooden horse. Demodocus sings how the Achaeans burn their camp and sail away, while Odysseus and others sit hidden in the horse, which the Trojans have dragged into their citadel. After long debate the Trojans keep it as an offering to the gods. The Achaeans pour out and sack Troy, and Odysseus, with Menelaus, wins his hardest fight at the house of Deiphobus.

8.10.title: Alcinous asks his guest's name
8.10.text: Odysseus weeps as he listens, and only Alcinous notices. The king stops the song and asks the stranger his name and country, so that the Phaeacian ships, which need no steersmen, can take him there. He recalls his father Nausithous' warning that Poseidon will one day wreck a Phaeacian ship on its way home and hide the city behind a mountain. He also asks where he has wandered and why the fate of the Achaeans and of Troy makes him weep.

9.1.title: Odysseus tells his name
9.1.text: In the hall of Alcinous, Odysseus tells the Phaeacians who he is: Odysseus, son of Laertes, from Ithaca. He describes his island, with Mount Neriton and the neighbouring islands Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus. Nothing, he says, is sweeter to a man than his own land. Then he begins the story of his voyage home from Troy.

9.2.title: The Cicones at Ismarus
9.2.text: From Troy the wind carries Odysseus' ships to Ismarus, the town of the Cicones. The Achaeans sack it and share out the women and the plunder. Odysseus orders them to leave at once, but the men stay on the shore, drinking and slaughtering sheep and cattle. In the morning more Cicones arrive from inland, and by evening they rout the Achaeans; six men from each ship are killed.

9.3.title: Past Malea to the Lotus-eaters
9.3.text: A storm from the north tears the sails, and the ships wait two days by the shore. At Cape Malea the current and the North Wind push them off course, past Cythera. For nine days the winds carry them, and on the tenth they land in the country of the Lotus-eaters. Three scouts eat the lotus and forget about going home; Odysseus drags them back to the ships, ties them under the benches and sails at once.

9.4.title: Goat Island
9.4.text: Odysseus comes to the land of the Cyclopes, who do not plough, have no laws or assemblies and live in mountain caves. Off the coast lies a wooded island of wild goats; the Cyclopes have no ships and never go there. The fleet runs ashore on it in a dark, misty night. Next day the crews of the twelve ships hunt goats and feast till sunset, and across the water they see the smoke of the Cyclopes and hear their flocks.

9.5.title: Into the Cyclops' cave
9.5.text: At dawn Odysseus leaves the other ships at the island and crosses to the land of the Cyclopes with his own. Near the shore stands a high cave with a walled yard, the home of a giant who herds his flocks alone. Odysseus goes there with twelve men and a skin of strong wine, a gift from Maron, priest of Apollo at Ismarus. The cave is empty; the men beg him to take the cheeses and lambs and go, but he wants to meet the owner.

9.6.title: The Cyclops comes home
9.6.text: The Cyclops Polyphemus comes back with his flocks and shuts the cave with a rock that twenty-two wagons could not move. He notices the strangers, and Odysseus asks him in the name of Zeus for a guest's welcome. The Cyclops answers that his kind care nothing for the gods, kills two of the men and eats them. While he sleeps Odysseus thinks of stabbing him, but holds back: they could never move the rock from the door.

9.7.title: The stake and the wine
9.7.text: At dawn the Cyclops eats two more men and drives his flocks out, closing the cave behind him. Odysseus cuts a stake from the giant's olive-wood club and hardens its point in the fire; four men are chosen by lot to help him. In the evening the Cyclops eats two more, and Odysseus gives him three bowls of the strong wine. He says his name is Nobody; the Cyclops promises to eat Nobody last and falls into a drunken sleep.

9.8.title: The blinding of Polyphemus
9.8.text: Odysseus heats the stake in the embers. With his four men he drives it into the eye of the sleeping Cyclops and twists it round. The Cyclops screams, and the other Cyclopes come running to the cave and ask Polyphemus who is hurting him. He answers that Nobody is killing him; they take it for an illness sent by Zeus, tell him to pray to his father Poseidon and go away.

9.9.title: Out under the rams
9.9.text: Blind Polyphemus pulls the rock away and sits in the doorway with his arms spread to catch the men. Odysseus ties the rams together in threes, a man under each middle one, and clings beneath the biggest ram himself. At dawn the flock goes out; Polyphemus feels only the backs of the animals and lets them pass. Outside Odysseus unties his men, and they drive the sheep to the ship and row away.

9.10.title: The curse of Polyphemus
9.10.text: From the ship Odysseus mocks Polyphemus, who hurls a rock that washes them back towards the shore. Against his men's pleas Odysseus shouts his real name and his home, Ithaca. Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon that Odysseus may never reach home, or may come late and alone, on a foreign ship, to trouble in his house; the god hears him. At the island they share out the sheep and sacrifice the ram to Zeus, and at dawn the fleet sails on.

10.1.title: The bag of winds
10.1.text: The ships reach Aeolia, a floating island walled with bronze, where Aeolus lives with his six sons and six daughters. He entertains Odysseus for a month and asks about Troy and the return of the Achaeans. When Odysseus asks to leave, Aeolus, the keeper of the winds, ties them up in an oxhide bag and fastens it in the ship. He lets only the West Wind blow, to carry them home.

10.2.title: Ithaca in sight
10.2.text: For nine days and nights the West Wind carries the ships. On the tenth day their own country comes in sight, so close that they can see men tending fires. Odysseus, who has held the sail-rope himself the whole way, falls asleep. The crew tell one another that the bag is full of gold and silver from Aeolus, and they want to see what is inside.

10.3.title: Blown back to Aeolia
10.3.text: The men untie the bag and all the winds rush out. A storm sweeps the ships away from their homeland and back to the island of Aeolus; Odysseus wakes, thinks of throwing himself into the sea, but endures. He goes to the house of Aeolus and asks for help again. Aeolus refuses to help a man the gods hate and orders him off the island.

10.4.title: Among the Laestrygonians
10.4.text: With no wind, the crews row for six days and on the seventh reach Telepylus, the town of the Laestrygonians. All the ships moor inside the narrow harbour among the cliffs; Odysseus alone ties up outside. Three scouts find the house of King Antiphates, who seizes one of them to eat. The Laestrygonians, huge as giants, crush the ships in the harbour with rocks and spear the men for food; only Odysseus' ship escapes.

10.5.title: Landing on Aeaea
10.5.text: The one ship left comes to Aeaea, the island of the goddess Circe, daughter of Helios. The men lie on the beach for two days, worn out with grief. On the third day Odysseus climbs a height and sees smoke rising from among the trees. On the way back he spears a great stag and carries it to the ship, and the crew feast until dark.

10.6.title: Circe turns men into swine
10.6.text: Next morning Odysseus tells the crew about the smoke and divides them into two bands. The lot falls to Eurylochus, who sets out with twenty-two men and finds Circe's house, where bewitched wolves and lions fawn on them. Circe invites them in, gives them a drugged drink, strikes them with her wand and shuts them in the sty as pigs with human minds. Eurylochus, who stayed outside, runs back to the ship with the news.

10.7.title: Hermes and the herb moly
10.7.text: Odysseus sets out alone for Circe's house, though Eurylochus begs him to flee. On the way Hermes, in the form of a young man, gives him the herb moly against her drugs and tells him what to do. Circe's drink has no effect on him, and when she strikes him with her wand he rushes at her with his sword. She guesses that he is Odysseus, invites him to her bed, and at his demand swears to do him no harm.

10.8.title: A year with Circe
10.8.text: Circe's maids bathe Odysseus and set a meal before him, but he will not eat until his men are free. Circe drives the swine out of the sty and smears them with another drug, and they become men again, younger and taller than before. Odysseus fetches the rest of the crew from the ship, although Eurylochus warns them not to go. They all stay in Circe's house for a full year, feasting.

10.9.title: The way to Hades
10.9.text: After a year the crew remind Odysseus of home, and he asks Circe to let them go. She agrees, but first he must go to the house of Hades and question the soul of the blind seer Tiresias of Thebes. The North Wind, she says, will carry the ship across Ocean to the groves of Persephone. There he must dig a pit, pour offerings to the dead, kill a ram and a black ewe and keep the souls from the blood until Tiresias has spoken.

10.10.title: Elpenor falls from the roof
10.10.text: At dawn Odysseus wakes his men and tells them to get ready. Elpenor, the youngest, has been sleeping off his wine on the roof of Circe's house; startled by the noise, he forgets the ladder, falls and breaks his neck. Odysseus then tells the crew that they are not going home but to the house of Hades, and they weep. At the ship they find a ram and a black ewe that Circe has tied there without being seen.

11.1.title: The rite at the trench
11.1.text: With a wind sent by Circe the ship sails all day and at sunset reaches the limits of Ocean, where the Cimmerians live in mist and darkness. Odysseus walks along the stream to the place Circe described, digs a pit, pours offerings to the dead and cuts the throats of the sheep over it. The souls of the dead swarm up out of Erebus with a great cry. He draws his sword and keeps them from the blood until he has questioned Tiresias.

11.2.title: Elpenor asks for burial
11.2.text: The first soul to come is that of Elpenor, whose body still lies unburied in Circe's house. He tells Odysseus how he fell from the roof and broke his neck. He begs him, when the ship puts in at Aeaea again, to burn his body with his armour, raise a mound on the shore and plant his oar on it. Odysseus promises to do so.

11.3.title: The prophecy of Tiresias
11.3.text: The soul of the seer Tiresias of Thebes comes and drinks the blood. He foretells that Poseidon, angry over his blinded son, will make the voyage hard. If the cattle of Helios on Thrinacia are not harmed, all may reach Ithaca; otherwise Odysseus will come home late and alone and find men courting his wife. Later, the seer says, he must carry an oar far inland and sacrifice to Poseidon, and death will come gently in old age.

11.4.title: Odysseus and his mother
11.4.text: Odysseus' mother Anticleia drinks the blood and knows her son. She tells him that Penelope still waits in the house, weeping, that Telemachus keeps the estate, and that Laertes lives on his farm in rags and never comes to town. She herself died of longing for Odysseus. Three times he tries to embrace her and three times she slips from his arms; this, she says, is what becomes of the dead.

11.5.title: Wives and daughters of heroes
11.5.text: Persephone sends up the souls of heroes' wives and daughters, and Odysseus lets them drink one at a time and tell who they are. He sees Tyro, who bore Poseidon the sons Pelias and Neleus of Pylos; Antiope, whose sons walled Thebes; and Epicaste, who unknowingly married her own son Oedipus. He sees Alcmene, Leda, and Ariadne, whom Theseus tried to take from Crete to Athens. Then Odysseus stops: it is time to sleep, he tells the Phaeacians.

11.6.title: The Phaeacians ask for more
11.6.text: In the hall on Scheria everyone sits silent, held by the story. Queen Arete praises the guest and asks the Phaeacians not to hurry him away or stint their gifts. Old Echeneus and Alcinous agree, and Alcinous asks Odysseus to stay until the next day. He says that Odysseus tells his tale like a bard and asks whether he saw any of his comrades from Troy among the dead, and Odysseus agrees to go on.

11.7.title: Agamemnon tells of his death
11.7.text: The soul of Agamemnon comes with those who died beside him. He tells how Aegisthus invited him to his house and, with Clytemnestra's help, killed him and his companions at the feast; Clytemnestra herself killed Cassandra. He advises Odysseus not to tell even his wife everything and to land in secret, though Penelope, he says, is wise and will not harm him. He asks for news of his son Orestes, but Odysseus has none.

11.8.title: Achilles among the dead
11.8.text: The soul of Achilles comes with those of Patroclus, Antilochus and Ajax. When Odysseus calls him a lord among the dead, Achilles answers that he would rather serve a poor man on earth than rule all the dead. He asks about his father Peleus in Phthia and about his son. Odysseus knows nothing of Peleus but tells how bravely Neoptolemus fought at Troy and waited in the wooden horse, and Achilles strides away glad.

11.9.title: The silence of Ajax
11.9.text: The other souls ask Odysseus about those they loved. Only the soul of Ajax, son of Telamon, stands apart, still angry that the arms of Achilles were awarded to Odysseus and not to him. Odysseus speaks to him gently, blames Zeus for the quarrel and asks him to come nearer. Ajax does not answer and walks away into Erebus with the other dead.

11.10.title: Minos, the punished and Heracles
11.10.text: Odysseus sees Minos judging the dead and Orion driving wild beasts over the meadow. He sees Tityus torn by two vultures, Tantalus reaching in vain for water and fruit, and Sisyphus pushing a stone that always rolls back. The phantom of Heracles tells how he was once sent here to fetch the hound of Hades. Then the dead crowd in with a great cry; Odysseus takes fright and hurries to the ship, and the crew row away down the stream of Ocean.

12.1.title: The burial of Elpenor
12.1.text: The ship leaves the stream of Ocean and returns over the sea to Aeaea. At dawn the men fetch Elpenor's body from Circe's house, burn it with his armour on the headland, heap a mound and plant his oar on top. Circe comes with her maids, bringing bread, meat and wine, and the crew feast all day. At night she takes Odysseus aside and he tells her everything.

12.2.title: Circe warns of the Sirens
12.2.text: Circe tells Odysseus what lies ahead. First come the Sirens, who sit in a meadow among men's bones and bewitch all who hear their song: he must plug the crew's ears with wax, and if he wants to listen he must be tied to the mast. After them he has to choose between two ways. One passes the Wandering Rocks, where surf and fire wreck every ship; only the Argo ever came through.

12.3.title: Circe warns of Scylla
12.3.text: The other way, Circe says, runs between two cliffs. In a cave in the higher one lives Scylla, a monster with six heads that each snatch a man from a passing ship; under the lower one Charybdis swallows the sea three times a day. He must keep to Scylla's side and not fight her: better to lose six men than all. Beyond lies Thrinacia, where the cattle of Helios graze; if they are harmed, she foretells the loss of ship and crew.

12.4.title: The song of the Sirens
12.4.text: At dawn the ship leaves Aeaea with a wind sent by Circe, and Odysseus tells the crew what she said about the Sirens. Near their island the wind drops and the men row. Odysseus plugs their ears with wax, and they tie him to the mast. The Sirens call him by name and promise to sing of Troy and of all that happens on earth; he signals to be set free, but Perimedes and Eurylochus tie him tighter until the ship is past.

12.5.title: Scylla takes six men
12.5.text: Past the island they meet smoke, heavy surf and a roar, and the men drop their oars in fear. Odysseus encourages them and tells the helmsman to keep clear of the surf and hug the cliff, but says nothing of Scylla. He arms himself, forgetting Circe's advice, and looks for Scylla in vain. While everyone stares at Charybdis sucking down the sea, Scylla snatches six of the best men from the ship and eats them at the mouth of her cave.

12.6.title: Landing on Thrinacia
12.6.text: The ship comes to Thrinacia, and from the sea Odysseus already hears the cattle and sheep of Helios. Remembering the warnings of Tiresias and Circe, he tells the crew to row past the island. Eurylochus objects that the men are exhausted and night is falling, and the others side with him. Odysseus makes them swear not to kill a single cow or sheep, and they land; in the night Zeus sends a storm, and at dawn they drag the ship into a cave.

12.7.title: The cattle of Helios
12.7.text: For a month the South Wind keeps the ship on the island, and when the stores run out the men go hungry. While Odysseus is away praying and falls asleep, Eurylochus persuades them to kill the best of the cattle of Helios. Lampetie brings the news to Helios, who demands vengeance, and Zeus promises to strike the ship with a thunderbolt. The men feast for six days; on the seventh the wind drops and they put to sea.

12.8.title: Shipwreck and Charybdis
12.8.text: Out of sight of land Zeus covers the ship with a dark cloud, and the West Wind strikes. The mast falls and kills the helmsman; a thunderbolt shatters the ship, and the whole crew is swept into the sea. Odysseus lashes keel and mast together and rides on them. The South Wind carries him back to Charybdis, where he hangs from the fig tree until she throws the timbers up again, then drops onto them and paddles away with his hands.

12.9.title: Nine days to Ogygia
12.9.text: For nine days Odysseus drifts on the timbers. On the tenth night the gods bring him to Ogygia, the island of Calypso, who takes him in and cares for him. Here Odysseus ends his tale: the rest he told Alcinous and Arete the day before.

13.1.title: Farewell to the Phaeacians
13.1.text: In the palace on Scheria Alcinous tells each of the Phaeacian elders to add a tripod and a cauldron to Odysseus' gifts. At dawn the gifts are stowed on the ship, and Alcinous sacrifices a bull to Zeus for a feast. Odysseus keeps turning towards the sun and waits for it to set. At sunset he takes leave of Alcinous, the Phaeacians pour wine to the gods, and Odysseus puts the cup into Arete's hand and wishes her well.

13.2.title: The night voyage
13.2.text: Odysseus leaves the palace of Alcinous, and a herald leads him down to the ship. Arete's maids carry a cloak and a tunic, a chest, bread and wine. The Phaeacian crew make a bed for him on the stern deck, and as soon as they begin to row he falls into a deep sleep. The ship runs through the night, faster than a hawk can fly, and when the morning star rises it draws near to Ithaca.

13.3.title: The harbour of Phorcys
13.3.text: On Ithaca there is a harbour of Phorcys, the old man of the sea, sheltered by two headlands. At its head stands an olive tree, and beside it is a cave sacred to the nymphs, with one entrance for men and one for the gods. The Phaeacians row in so fast that the ship runs half its length up the beach. They lift the sleeping Odysseus onto the sand and pile his gifts by the olive tree, away from the path.

13.4.title: The ship turned to stone
13.4.text: While the Phaeacians sail home, Poseidon complains to Zeus that they have brought Odysseus to Ithaca with rich gifts, and Zeus lets him punish them. Off Scheria, in sight of the town, Poseidon strikes the ship with his hand and turns it to stone. Alcinous recalls his father's prophecy and orders the Phaeacians to carry no more strangers home and to offer Poseidon twelve bulls, so that he does not cover the town with a mountain.

13.5.title: Odysseus wakes on Ithaca
13.5.text: Odysseus wakes on the shore of his own land and does not know it, because Athena has poured a mist around him. He thinks the Phaeacians have left him in a strange country, and he counts his tripods, cauldrons, gold and clothes: nothing is missing. Athena comes to him in the shape of a young shepherd. He asks what land this is, and she tells him that it is Ithaca.

13.6.title: A false tale for Athena
13.6.text: Odysseus is glad to hear the name of Ithaca, but he hides who he is and makes up a story for the shepherd. He says he is a Cretan who killed a son of Idomeneus in a night ambush, because the man wanted to take his booty from Troy. In his story he paid Phoenician sailors to carry him to Pylos or Elis, but the wind drove them here. They set him ashore asleep with his goods and sailed on to Sidon.

13.7.title: Athena shows herself
13.7.text: Athena smiles, strokes Odysseus with her hand and takes the shape of a tall and beautiful woman. She tells him who she is and says that no one can outdo him in tricks. She has come to make a plan with him and to hide his treasure, and she warns him to tell no one that he is back and to bear insults in silence. Odysseus still doubts that this is Ithaca and begs her to tell him the truth.

13.8.title: The mist lifts
13.8.text: Athena tells Odysseus that she always knew he would come home but did not want to fight her uncle Poseidon. She points out the harbour of Phorcys, the olive tree, the cave of the nymphs and Mount Neriton, and scatters the mist. Odysseus recognises his land, kisses the earth and prays to the nymphs. He carries the gold, bronze and clothes into the cave, and Athena closes the entrance with a stone.

13.9.title: The plan and the disguise
13.9.text: Odysseus and Athena sit down by the olive tree and plan the death of the suitors. She tells him that for three years they have lorded it in his hall and courted Penelope, and promises to stand beside him. She sends him first to the swineherd, whose pigs feed by the Raven's Rock and the spring Arethusa; she herself will go to Sparta to call Telemachus home. With her wand she turns him into an old beggar in rags, and they part.

14.1.title: The walk to the swineherd
14.1.text: Odysseus, disguised as an old beggar, climbs the rough path from the harbour through the wooded hills. He finds the swineherd sitting in front of the farmstead, a high-walled yard with twelve sties that he built himself. The dogs rush at the stranger, and Odysseus sits down and lets his staff fall. The swineherd drives them off with stones, speaks of his grief for his lost master and asks the old man into his hut.

14.2.title: Eumaeus welcomes the stranger
14.2.text: The swineherd Eumaeus seats Odysseus on a goatskin in his hut and says that all strangers and beggars come from Zeus. He kills two young pigs, roasts them and serves them with wine. The fat hogs, he says, go to the suitors, who eat up his master's herds day after day. Odysseus eats in silence and thinks of how to harm the suitors.

14.3.title: The lost master
14.3.text: After the meal Odysseus asks who the master was. Eumaeus says that wanderers lie to Penelope for a cloak and that his master is surely dead; then he names him: Odysseus. Odysseus, in disguise, swears that the master will be home at the change of the moon and will take revenge. Eumaeus does not believe it; he fears for Telemachus, who has gone to Pylos while the suitors lie in wait for him, and asks the stranger who he is.

14.4.title: The tale of the Cretan
14.4.text: Odysseus answers with an invented life story. He says he is from Crete, the son of a rich man and a bought slave woman. When the father died, the lawful sons gave him only a small share, but he married into a wealthy house because he was a brave fighter. He never cared for farm work, only for ships, war and spears, and nine raids across the sea made him rich and respected among the Cretans.

14.5.title: The raid on Egypt
14.5.text: Odysseus goes on with his invented tale. He says he led the Cretan ships to Troy together with Idomeneus and came home after ten years. Only a month later he sailed with nine ships to Egypt and anchored in the river Aigyptos. His men plundered the fields, the Egyptians came out at dawn and killed or enslaved them, and he threw down his arms and begged the king for mercy; the king spared him and took him home.

14.6.title: Phoenicia and the shipwreck
14.6.text: The tale goes on: he stayed seven years in Egypt and grew rich. A Phoenician cheat then took him to Phoenicia and a year later put him on a ship for Libya, meaning to sell him there. Beyond Crete Zeus struck the ship with a thunderbolt and the whole crew was lost. He drifted on the mast for nine days, and on the tenth night the waves cast him on the land of the Thesprotians, where the king took him in.

14.7.title: False news of Odysseus
14.7.text: The tale ends with news of Odysseus. The Thesprotian king, the stranger says, had been host to Odysseus and was keeping his treasure; Odysseus himself had gone to Dodona to ask the oak of Zeus how to come home. The king put the stranger on a ship for Dulichium, but the crew stripped him, put him in rags and tied him up. When they landed on Ithaca at evening he got free, swam away and hid, and so reached the farmstead.

14.8.title: Eumaeus does not believe
14.8.text: Eumaeus is moved by the stranger's sufferings but does not believe what he says about Odysseus. He tells how an Aetolian once deceived him with the news that Odysseus was in Crete with Idomeneus, mending his ships. Odysseus offers a bargain: a cloak and passage to Dulichium if the master returns, and death from a high rock if he does not. Eumaeus refuses to kill a guest and says it is time for supper.

14.9.title: A boar for the stranger
14.9.text: When the other swineherds come back with the herds, Eumaeus has them bring the best boar, a five-year-old, for the guest. He throws bristles from its head into the fire and prays to all the gods that Odysseus may come home. He divides the meat into seven portions, sets one aside for the nymphs and Hermes, and honours Odysseus with the long back cut. The bread is served by a slave whom Eumaeus himself bought from the Taphians.

14.10.title: The story of the cloak
14.10.text: The night is dark, wet and windy. To test Eumaeus, Odysseus tells how he once lay in ambush under the walls of Troy on a freezing night with no cloak. In the story his leader Odysseus sent a man running to the ships with a made-up message, and the man left his cloak behind. Eumaeus understands: he makes a bed by the fire, covers the stranger with his own thick cloak and goes out to sleep beside the boars under a rock.

15.1.title: Athena in Sparta
15.1.text: Athena comes to Sparta and finds Telemachus lying awake in the porch of Menelaus' palace. She tells him to go home, because Penelope's father and brothers want her to marry Eurymachus. She warns him that suitors lie in wait in the strait between Ithaca and Same; he must sail by night, land on the nearest shore of Ithaca and go first to the swineherd. Telemachus wakes Peisistratus, who says they must wait for daylight.

15.2.title: Menelaus' parting gifts
15.2.text: At dawn Telemachus asks Menelaus to let him go home. Menelaus agrees, orders a meal and goes down to the storeroom with Helen and Megapenthes. He gives Telemachus a two-handled cup and a silver mixing bowl that he once received from the king of the Sidonians. Helen gives him a robe she made herself, for his bride to wear on her wedding day.

15.3.title: The eagle and the goose
15.3.text: After the meal Telemachus and Peisistratus mount the chariot in front of Menelaus' palace. Menelaus brings wine for a parting libation and sends greetings to Nestor. An eagle flies past on the right with a white goose from the yard in its claws. Helen explains the sign: as the eagle seized the goose, so Odysseus will come home and take revenge, or he is home already.

15.4.title: The road back to Pylos
15.4.text: Telemachus and Peisistratus drive all day and spend the night at Pherae in the house of Diocles. The next day they reach Pylos. Telemachus asks his friend to take him straight to the ship, so that Nestor does not keep him as a guest. Peisistratus drives to the shore, puts the gifts of Menelaus on board and tells Telemachus to sail before the old man hears of it.

15.5.title: Theoclymenus comes aboard
15.5.text: While Telemachus prays to Athena beside his ship on the shore of Pylos, a stranger comes up: Theoclymenus, a seer, who has killed a man in Argos and is fleeing from the dead man's kin. He begs to be taken on board, and Telemachus agrees. Athena sends a fair wind. At nightfall the ship passes Pheae and Elis, and Telemachus steers for the Pointed Islands, wondering whether he will escape death or be caught.

15.6.title: Evening in Eumaeus' hut
15.6.text: Odysseus and Eumaeus are at supper in the hut on Ithaca. To test his host, Odysseus says he will go to town in the morning to beg and serve the suitors, and Eumaeus tells him to stay and wait for Telemachus. Asked about Odysseus' parents, he says that Laertes lives but prays for death, and that Anticleia died of grief for her son. She had brought Eumaeus up with her daughter Ctimene, who was married off to Same.

15.7.title: Eumaeus tells his story
15.7.text: Odysseus asks how Eumaeus came to Ithaca as a child. Eumaeus tells him that his father was king of the two towns on the island of Syrie. Phoenician traders came there, and one of them seduced a Phoenician slave woman in the king's house, whom Taphian pirates had once stolen from Sidon. She agreed to sail home with them and promised to bring gold and the king's small son, whom she nursed, as payment for her passage.

15.8.title: Eumaeus is carried off
15.8.text: Eumaeus goes on: the Phoenicians traded on Syrie for a year, and when the ship was full a man came to the palace with a gold and amber necklace and nodded to the nurse. She took the boy, hid three cups in her dress and led him to the harbour at sunset. On the seventh day at sea Artemis struck her dead, and wind and wave brought the ship to Ithaca, where Laertes bought the child. Then the two men sleep a short while.

15.9.title: Telemachus lands on Ithaca
15.9.text: At dawn the ship of Telemachus reaches the shore of Ithaca, and the crew eat on the beach. Telemachus tells them to row on to the town, while he goes to see his fields and herdsmen. Theoclymenus asks whose house he should go to. Telemachus says his own house is no place for a guest while he is away, and names Eurymachus, the foremost of the suitors.

15.10.title: The hawk and the dove
15.10.text: As Telemachus speaks, a hawk flies past on the right, tearing a dove in its claws. Theoclymenus takes him aside and says the sign means that no family on Ithaca is more kingly than his. Telemachus now asks his friend Peiraeus to take the seer into his own house. The ship sails on to the town, and Telemachus walks quickly to the farmstead of the swineherd.

16.1.title: Telemachus at the farmstead
16.1.text: At dawn Odysseus and Eumaeus are making breakfast in the hut when Telemachus comes to the door; the dogs do not bark but fawn on him. Eumaeus drops the bowls, kisses him and weeps like a father whose son is home after ten years. Telemachus asks whether his mother is still in the palace, and Eumaeus says she is. Odysseus, still in the shape of a beggar, offers his seat, but Telemachus tells the stranger to stay seated.

16.2.title: Telemachus and the stranger
16.2.text: After the meal Telemachus asks Eumaeus where the stranger comes from. Eumaeus says he is a Cretan wanderer who escaped from a Thesprotian ship, and puts him in Telemachus' hands as a suppliant. Telemachus answers that in his own house he cannot protect a guest from the suitors. He will give the stranger a cloak, a tunic, a sword and sandals, or send clothes and food to the farmstead if Eumaeus keeps him there.

16.3.title: Eumaeus is sent to Penelope
16.3.text: Odysseus, as the stranger, says that in Telemachus' place he would fight the suitors or die in his own hall. Telemachus explains that he has no brothers to help him, and that nobles from Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus and Ithaca fill the house and court his mother. He sends Eumaeus to tell Penelope, and no one else, that he is back from Pylos. Eumaeus picks up his sandals to set out for the town.

16.4.title: Father and son
16.4.text: When Eumaeus has left, Athena appears outside the hut; only Odysseus and the dogs see her. She tells him to reveal himself to his son, touches him with her golden wand and makes him tall, strong and well dressed again. Telemachus takes him for a god, and Odysseus says that he is his father. Telemachus does not believe it until Odysseus explains that the change is Athena's work; then they embrace and weep aloud.

16.5.title: Counting the suitors
16.5.text: Odysseus tells his son that the Phaeacians brought him to Ithaca asleep and that their gifts lie hidden in a cave. He asks how many the suitors are. Telemachus counts fifty-two from Dulichium, twenty-four from Same, twenty from Zacynthus and twelve from Ithaca, with servants, the herald Medon and the bard. He says two men cannot fight so many, and Odysseus answers that Athena and Zeus will help them.

16.6.title: Odysseus lays out his plan
16.6.text: Odysseus tells Telemachus to go home at dawn and join the suitors. He himself will come to the town later with the swineherd, as an old beggar, and his son must bear it if the suitors abuse him. At a nod from his father Telemachus is to carry the weapons from the hall to the storeroom and leave only two swords, two spears and two shields. No one may learn that Odysseus is back, not Laertes, not Eumaeus, not even Penelope.

16.7.title: Two ships in the harbour
16.7.text: The ship that carried Telemachus from Pylos puts in at the harbour of the town. A herald from the crew and Eumaeus both bring Penelope the news that her son is back, and Eumaeus returns to his pigs. The suitors are dismayed and gather in front of the palace gate. Eurymachus wants to send a ship to call the ambush home, but Amphinomus sees their ship already in the harbour, and they go down to the shore.

16.8.title: The suitors plot again
16.8.text: The suitors go to the assembly place and let no one else sit with them. Antinous says a god has saved Telemachus from their ambush; he proposes to kill him in the fields or on the road before he can call the people together, and to divide his goods. Amphinomus of Dulichium answers that it is a terrible thing to kill a man of royal blood and that they must first ask the will of the gods. The suitors agree and go back to the palace.

16.9.title: Penelope faces the suitors
16.9.text: Penelope learns of the plot from the herald Medon. She comes down to the hall and rebukes Antinous: his father once fled to this house after raiding the Thesprotians with Taphian pirates, and Odysseus saved him from the angry people. Eurymachus answers that no one will lay a hand on Telemachus while he lives, but he himself is planning the murder. Penelope goes up to her room and weeps for Odysseus until Athena sends her sleep.

16.10.title: Eumaeus returns at evening
16.10.text: In the evening Eumaeus comes back to the farmstead. Athena touches Odysseus with her wand and makes him an old beggar again, so that the swineherd does not recognise him. Eumaeus reports that from the hill of Hermes above the town he saw a ship full of armed men come into the harbour. Telemachus smiles and glances at his father; then they eat and go to sleep.

17.1.title: Telemachus comes home
17.1.text: At dawn Telemachus leaves the farmstead for the town and tells Eumaeus to bring the stranger there to beg. Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, says he will follow once the sun has warmed the day. In the palace the nurse Eurycleia is the first to see Telemachus, and Penelope embraces him in tears. He asks her to wash and vow sacrifices to the gods, and says he is going to fetch a guest.

17.2.title: At the assembly place
17.2.text: Telemachus walks to the assembly place with his spear and two dogs, and Athena makes all the people admire him. The suitors crowd round him with friendly words, but he sits down with Mentor and Halitherses, old friends of his father. Peiraeus brings the seer Theoclymenus and offers to send over the gifts from Menelaus. Telemachus, who fears that the suitors may kill him, asks Peiraeus to keep them for now and leads his guest home.

17.3.title: Telemachus tells of his journey
17.3.text: In the palace Telemachus and Theoclymenus eat, and Penelope asks her son for news of Odysseus. Telemachus says that Nestor at Pylos knew nothing, but Menelaus in Sparta had heard from Proteus that the nymph Calypso keeps Odysseus on her island. Theoclymenus swears that Odysseus is already in his own land, preparing evil for the suitors. Outside, the suitors throw discus and javelin until the herald Medon calls them to dinner.

17.4.title: Melanthius at the fountain
17.4.text: Eumaeus gives Odysseus a staff and leads him, in his beggar's rags, along the rough path to the town. At the fountain of the nymphs, where the townspeople draw water, they meet the goatherd Melanthius driving goats for the suitors' dinner. Melanthius insults them both and kicks Odysseus on the hip. Odysseus thinks of killing him but holds back, and Eumaeus prays to the nymphs that his master may come home.

17.5.title: The dog Argus
17.5.text: Melanthius hurries ahead and sits down among the suitors, opposite Eurymachus. Odysseus and Eumaeus stop in front of the palace, where the bard Phemius is playing, and agree that Eumaeus will go in first. A dog lying on the dung heap by the doors lifts his head: it is Argus, whom Odysseus raised before he left for Troy. He wags his tail but is too weak to come closer; Odysseus secretly wipes away a tear, and Argus dies.

17.6.title: Odysseus begs among the suitors
17.6.text: Eumaeus sits down at the table of Telemachus, and Odysseus, in his beggar's rags, takes a place on the threshold of the hall. Telemachus sends him bread and meat, and Athena urges him to beg from every suitor, to learn which of them are decent. The suitors pity him and give; only Antinous scolds Eumaeus for bringing a beggar, argues with Telemachus and shows the footstool he keeps under his table.

17.7.title: Antinous throws a footstool
17.7.text: Odysseus stops before Antinous and tells a false tale: once a rich man, he sailed to Egypt with pirates, was captured and handed over to the ruler of Cyprus. Antinous orders him off, and when Odysseus answers back he throws the footstool and hits his right shoulder. Odysseus stands like a rock, then sits down on the threshold and wishes Antinous dead before his wedding. The other suitors blame Antinous: the stranger may be a god.

17.8.title: Penelope sends for the beggar
17.8.text: In her room Penelope hears that the stranger has been struck and wishes Apollo would strike Antinous the same way. She sends Eumaeus to bring the beggar, to ask him about Odysseus. Eumaeus says the man comes from Crete and claims to have heard that Odysseus is alive among the Thesprotians. Telemachus sneezes loudly in the hall, and Penelope laughs: she takes it as a sign that her words about the suitors will come true.

17.9.title: Odysseus asks Penelope to wait
17.9.text: Eumaeus brings Penelope's message, but Odysseus is wary of the suitors and asks her to wait until sunset; then he will tell her about her husband by the fire. Penelope finds the stranger's answer wise. Eumaeus whispers to Telemachus to look after himself and, after eating, goes back to his pigs; Telemachus tells him to return at dawn with animals for sacrifice. The suitors dance and sing as evening comes on.

18.1.title: Irus the beggar
18.1.text: A beggar known all over the town comes to the palace: a big, greedy man whom the young men call Irus because he carries their messages. He orders Odysseus off the threshold and threatens to drag him out by the foot. Odysseus, disguised as an old beggar, answers that the threshold has room for both of them and warns him not to start a fight. Irus challenges him to gird himself and fight.

18.2.title: The fight with Irus
18.2.text: Antinous laughs and sets the two beggars to fight, with a goat's paunch full of fat and blood as the prize. The suitors swear not to strike the stranger to help Irus, and Telemachus promises to stand by him. When Odysseus girds up his rags and shows his strong thighs and shoulders, Irus shakes with fear. Odysseus fells him with one blow under the ear, drags him out into the courtyard and props him against the wall.

18.3.title: A warning to Amphinomus
18.3.text: Antinous sets the paunch before Odysseus, and Amphinomus brings two loaves and drinks to him from a golden cup. Odysseus, still playing the beggar, praises Amphinomus as the son of a good and wealthy man of Dulichium and warns him that the master of this house is very near and will not part from the suitors without blood. He hopes a god will lead him home before then. Amphinomus walks back through the hall with a heavy heart and sits down again.

18.4.title: Penelope shows herself
18.4.text: Athena gives Penelope the wish to show herself to the suitors. While Penelope sleeps on her couch, the goddess makes her taller and more beautiful. Penelope comes down with two maids and stands by a pillar of the hall, and every suitor longs for her. She scolds Telemachus for letting the stranger be mistreated; he answers that the stranger beat Irus, and wishes the suitors were beaten in the same way.

18.5.title: Gifts for Penelope
18.5.text: Eurymachus praises Penelope's beauty. She replies that it left her when Odysseus sailed for Troy, and recalls his parting words: once their son has a beard, she should marry whom she wishes. She adds that proper suitors bring gifts and do not eat up another man's goods; Odysseus is glad that she draws gifts from them. The suitors send for a robe, a gold chain, earrings and a necklace, and Penelope takes the gifts upstairs.

18.6.title: Melantho insults the beggar
18.6.text: The suitors dance and sing until dark, and three braziers are set up to light the hall. Odysseus tells the maids to go and sit with their queen: he will tend the fires himself. Melantho, a maid whom Penelope raised and who is now the lover of Eurymachus, calls him drunk or mad and tells him to sleep somewhere else. Odysseus threatens to tell Telemachus, the maids run off in fear, and he stays to tend the braziers.

18.7.title: Eurymachus throws a footstool
18.7.text: Eurymachus mocks the beggar's bald head and offers him paid farm work, then says he is too lazy to take it. Odysseus answers that he would beat him at mowing, ploughing or fighting, and that the doors would be too narrow for Eurymachus if Odysseus came home. Eurymachus throws a footstool; Odysseus crouches at the knees of Amphinomus, and it hits the cupbearer. Telemachus tells the suitors to go home to bed, and after a libation they leave.

19.1.title: The weapons are removed
19.1.text: When the suitors have gone, Odysseus tells Telemachus to take all the weapons out of the hall and gives him an excuse for the suitors: the smoke was spoiling them. The nurse Eurycleia shuts the maids in their rooms. Father and son carry the helmets, shields and spears to the storeroom, and Athena goes before them with a golden lamp that lights up the walls. Odysseus sends Telemachus to bed and stays in the hall.

19.2.title: Penelope rebukes Melantho
19.2.text: Penelope comes from her room and sits by the fire in her chair inlaid with ivory and silver, while the maids clear the tables and build up the fires. Melantho again tells the beggar to get out of the house. Odysseus warns her that she may lose her place if her mistress grows angry or if Odysseus returns. Penelope hears him, rebukes Melantho sharply and has the housekeeper Eurynome bring a chair for the stranger.

19.3.title: Penelope tells of the web
19.3.text: Penelope asks the stranger who he is and where he comes from. Odysseus praises her fame and begs her not to ask about his family and homeland, because the memory pains him. She tells him how the nobles of Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus and Ithaca press her to marry. For three years she held them off by weaving a shroud for Laertes by day and unpicking it at night, until her maids betrayed her; now she sees no way out.

19.4.title: A false tale of Crete
19.4.text: Odysseus invents a story: he is Aethon of Knossos in Crete, grandson of Minos and younger brother of Idomeneus. A storm, he says, drove Odysseus past Malea to Amnisus on his way to Troy, and he entertained him for twelve days. Penelope weeps; Odysseus pities her but hides his own tears. To test him she asks what her husband wore, and he describes the purple cloak and the gold brooch of a hound gripping a fawn; she recognises them.

19.5.title: The beggar's oath
19.5.text: Still speaking as the Cretan, Odysseus tells Penelope that her husband is alive and close by, in the land of the Thesprotians, with great treasure. He says that Odysseus lost his ship and men after leaving Thrinacia, was washed ashore among the Phaeacians, and has now gone to Dodona to ask the oak of Zeus how to return. He swears by Zeus and by the hearth of Odysseus that Odysseus will come as this moon wanes and the next begins.

19.6.title: Penelope calls Eurycleia
19.6.text: Penelope wishes the oath were true but does not believe that Odysseus will come. She tells her maids to wash the stranger's feet and make up a bed for him. Odysseus refuses the blankets and will let only an old woman who has suffered as much as he has touch his feet, so Penelope calls the nurse Eurycleia. Eurycleia weeps for her lost master and says she has never seen a stranger so like Odysseus in build, voice and feet.

19.7.title: The scar from Parnassus
19.7.text: Eurycleia fills the basin, and Odysseus turns towards the dark, afraid that she will notice his scar. She recognises it as soon as she touches him. The scar comes from a boar hunt on Parnassus: as a young man Odysseus visited his grandfather Autolycus, who had given him his name, and a boar gashed him above the knee before he killed it with his spear. Autolycus and his sons healed the wound and sent him home to Ithaca with gifts.

19.8.title: Eurycleia knows her master
19.8.text: Eurycleia feels the scar and lets his foot fall, so that the bronze basin rings and the water spills. In tears she touches his chin and says that he is Odysseus. She looks towards Penelope, but Athena has turned Penelope's mind elsewhere. Odysseus grips the nurse by the throat and orders her to tell no one; she promises to be as hard as stone, washes his feet, and he covers the scar with his rags.

19.9.title: The dream of the geese
19.9.text: Penelope tells the stranger that at night her cares keep her awake: she cannot decide whether to stay and guard the house for her son or to marry the best of the suitors. She asks him to explain a dream. An eagle from the mountain killed her twenty geese, then spoke with a human voice and said that the geese were the suitors and he was her husband come home. Odysseus answers that the dream can mean only what the eagle said.

19.10.title: Penelope announces the contest
19.10.text: Penelope answers that false dreams come through a gate of ivory and true ones through a gate of horn, and she doubts hers was true. In the morning she will set the suitors a contest and marry the one who most easily strings the bow of Odysseus and shoots an arrow through twelve axes in a row. Odysseus urges her not to delay: Odysseus will be home before any of them strings the bow. Penelope goes upstairs and weeps until Athena sends her sleep.

20.1.title: Odysseus cannot sleep
20.1.text: Odysseus beds down in the entrance hall of the palace on an oxhide and fleeces, but he cannot sleep. He sees the maids who sleep with the suitors go out laughing, and he masters his anger by telling his heart that it endured worse in the cave of the Cyclops. He tosses and turns, wondering how one man can fight so many. Athena comes down in the form of a woman, promises her help and pours sleep on his eyes.

20.2.title: Prayers and signs at dawn
20.2.text: Penelope wakes and weeps in her bed. She prays to Artemis to kill her with an arrow, or for a storm wind to carry her away, so that she need never please a lesser man than Odysseus. At dawn Odysseus hears her weeping and asks Zeus for two signs. Zeus thunders from Olympus, and a woman still grinding grain at the mill prays that this may be the suitors' last feast in the house.

20.3.title: Morning in the palace
20.3.text: In the morning the maids light the hearth fire. Telemachus asks Eurycleia whether the guest was given food and a bed, then goes to the assembly place. Eurycleia sets the maids to sweep the hall, wipe the tables and fetch water: it is a feast day, and the suitors will come early. Eumaeus drives in three hogs and speaks kindly to Odysseus; Melanthius brings goats and threatens him with his fists, and Odysseus says nothing.

20.4.title: Philoetius the cowherd
20.4.text: A third herdsman arrives: the cowherd Philoetius, with a cow and goats that ferrymen have brought across the water. He greets the beggar kindly and weeps at the thought that Odysseus may be wandering in rags like these. He would have left with the cattle long ago, he says, if he did not still hope for his master's return.
