Odysseus swears that the master will come home while Philoetius is still here, and both herdsmen pray for it.

20.5.title: The feast begins
20.5.text: The suitors are plotting to kill Telemachus when an eagle flies past on their left holding a dove, and Amphinomus says the plan will fail. They go into the palace and slaughter animals for the feast; Eumaeus, Philoetius and Melanthius serve them. Telemachus seats Odysseus at a small table by the stone threshold and warns the suitors to keep their insults and their hands to themselves. Antinous tells the others to put up with it.

20.6.title: Ctesippus throws an ox foot
20.6.text: Ctesippus, a rich suitor from Same, says he too has a guest-gift for the stranger and throws an ox foot at him. Odysseus tilts his head aside, and it hits the wall. Telemachus tells Ctesippus that he would have speared him if he had hit the guest. Agelaus asks the suitors to leave the stranger alone and advises Telemachus to urge his mother to marry; Telemachus answers that he will not drive her out against her will.

20.7.title: The vision of Theoclymenus
20.7.text: Athena sends the suitors into wild laughter, but their eyes fill with tears and their meat is smeared with blood. The seer Theoclymenus sees night around their heads, blood on the walls and a courtyard full of ghosts, and warns that evil is coming for them all. They laugh at him, and he leaves for the house of Peiraeus. The suitors joke about selling Telemachus' guests to the Sicels; he silently watches his father, while Penelope listens nearby.

21.1.title: Penelope goes for the bow
21.1.text: Athena puts it in Penelope's mind to set the bow of Odysseus and the iron axes before the suitors as a contest. With her maids she goes to the farthest storeroom of the palace, where the bow lies. Iphitus gave it to the young Odysseus when they met in Messene, in Lacedaemon, and Odysseus never took it to war. Penelope lifts it from its peg, weeps over it and carries it to the hall.

21.2.title: The bow before the suitors
21.2.text: Penelope comes before the suitors in the hall with a maid on either side. She says she will marry the man who most easily strings the bow of Odysseus and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes. Eumaeus lays out the bow and the axes in tears, and the cowherd Philoetius weeps too. Antinous scolds the two herdsmen and says the bow will be hard to string, though he hopes to string it himself.

21.3.title: Telemachus tries the bow
21.3.text: Telemachus tells the suitors not to hang back and says he will try the bow himself. He digs one long trench, sets the axes in it in a straight line and stamps the earth down round them. From the threshold he tries three times to string the bow and fails. At the fourth pull he is about to succeed, but Odysseus signs to him to stop; Telemachus puts the bow down and tells the stronger men to try.

21.4.title: The suitors try in turn
21.4.text: Antinous has the suitors try in turn, from left to right. The seer Leodes goes first, but his soft hands tire before he can string the bow, and he says it will take the heart and life out of many nobles. Antinous rebukes him and has the goatherd Melanthius light a fire and bring tallow to warm and grease the bow. The young men try one after another and fail; only Antinous and Eurymachus, the strongest, are left.

21.5.title: The herdsmen learn the truth
21.5.text: Eumaeus and Philoetius leave the hall, and Odysseus follows them out past the courtyard gates. He asks whether they would fight for Odysseus if he came back, and both pray for his return. Then he tells them who he is and shows the scar a boar gave him on Parnassus; they weep and kiss him. He orders Eumaeus to bring him the bow and tell the women to lock the doors to their rooms, and Philoetius to bar the courtyard gate.

21.6.title: The contest is put off
21.6.text: In the hall Eurymachus warms the bow at the fire and still cannot string it. He groans that men to come will hear how much weaker the suitors are than Odysseus. Antinous answers that today is the holy feast of the god and no day for bending bows. He proposes to leave the axes standing, pour libations and try again tomorrow after sacrificing goats to Apollo; the suitors agree and drink.

21.7.title: The beggar's request
21.7.text: After the libation Odysseus, still in his beggar's rags, asks the suitors to let him try the bow. They fear he may string it, and Antinous threatens to send him by ship to king Echetus. Penelope says the stranger should have his turn and promises him clothes, a spear and a sword if he succeeds. Telemachus declares that the bow is his to give or refuse and sends his mother to her rooms, where Athena puts her to sleep.

21.8.title: The bow reaches Odysseus
21.8.text: Eumaeus picks up the bow, but the suitors shout at him and he puts it down in fright. Telemachus threatens him from the other side, the suitors laugh, and the swineherd carries the bow through the hall and puts it in Odysseus' hands. Then he tells the nurse Eurycleia to lock the doors to the women's rooms. Philoetius slips out, bars the courtyard gate, ties it with a ship's cable and returns to his seat.

21.9.title: Odysseus strings the bow
21.9.text: Odysseus turns the bow over in his hands to see whether worms have eaten the horn, while the suitors mock him. Then he strings it without effort and tries the string with his right hand. The suitors turn pale, and Zeus thunders. Without rising from his seat Odysseus shoots an arrow through all the axes; at his nod Telemachus girds on his sword, takes his spear and stands beside him.

22.1.title: Odysseus kills Antinous
22.1.text: Odysseus throws off his rags, leaps onto the great threshold with the bow and pours the arrows out at his feet. His first arrow goes through the throat of Antinous as he lifts a golden cup to drink. The suitors spring up and look along the walls for shields and spears, but there are none; they think the stranger has killed by accident and threaten him with death. Then Odysseus tells them who he is, and fear seizes them all.

22.2.title: Eurymachus offers to pay
22.2.text: Eurymachus alone answers. He puts all the blame on the dead Antinous and offers that each suitor repay Odysseus in bronze and gold to the worth of twenty oxen. Odysseus refuses any payment and tells them to fight or flee. Eurymachus calls on the suitors to draw their swords and shield themselves with the tables, and rushes at Odysseus; an arrow strikes him in the chest and he falls dead over his table.

22.3.title: Telemachus brings the arms
22.3.text: Amphinomus rushes at Odysseus with drawn sword, and Telemachus kills him with a spear in the back. Telemachus runs to the storeroom and brings four shields, eight spears and four helmets; he, Eumaeus and Philoetius arm and stand beside Odysseus. Odysseus shoots down one suitor after another until his arrows run out. Then he leans the bow against the doorpost, puts on shield and helmet and takes two spears.

22.4.title: Melanthius and the armour
22.4.text: Agelaus wants someone to slip out by the side door and rouse the town. The goatherd Melanthius says one man could bar that way; instead he climbs to the storeroom, whose door Telemachus left open, and brings the suitors twelve shields, spears and helmets. When he goes back for more, Eumaeus and Philoetius seize him there, bind his hands and feet behind him, as Odysseus ordered, and hoist him on a rope to the roof beams. Then they return to the threshold.

22.5.title: Athena in Mentor's shape
22.5.text: Athena comes to the threshold in the shape of Mentor, and Odysseus, guessing who it is, asks for help. Agelaus threatens Mentor with death and the ruin of his house if he fights for Odysseus. Athena angrily asks Odysseus where the strength has gone that he showed in nine years of war at Troy. She still holds back from deciding the fight and goes on testing him and his son, and flies up as a swallow to a roof beam of the hall.

22.6.title: The battle in the hall
22.6.text: Agelaus has six suitors throw their spears first, all at Odysseus, and Athena makes them miss. Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius throw in turn, and each kills his man. A second volley only grazes Telemachus' wrist and Eumaeus' shoulder; in answer Amphimedon, Ctesippus, Agelaus and Leocritus fall with others. Then Athena raises her aegis from the roof, the suitors run in panic through the hall, and the four strike them down.

22.7.title: Three men beg for mercy
22.7.text: The seer Leodes clasps Odysseus' knees and says he did no wrong in the house; Odysseus answers that he must have prayed against his return, and cuts off his head. The bard Phemius lays down his lyre and begs in his turn: the suitors made him sing by force. Telemachus speaks up for him and for the herald Medon, who crawls out from his hiding place under a chair. Odysseus spares both and sends them to sit by the altar of Zeus in the courtyard.

22.8.title: Eurycleia among the dead
22.8.text: Odysseus looks through the hall and sees that no suitor is left alive; they lie heaped in blood and dust. Telemachus calls the nurse Eurycleia, who finds Odysseus among the bodies, spattered with blood. She is about to cry out in triumph, but he stops her: it is not right to exult over dead men. Asked about the maids, she says that twelve of the fifty have behaved shamelessly; he sends her to fetch those twelve and tells her not to wake Penelope yet.

22.9.title: The maids and Melanthius
22.9.text: On Odysseus' orders the twelve maids carry the dead out to the portico of the courtyard and wash the chairs and tables, while Telemachus and the two herdsmen scrape the floor. Then Telemachus hangs the maids in the courtyard on a ship's cable. Melanthius is led out, and they cut off his nose, ears, hands and feet. Odysseus cleanses the hall and the courtyard with sulphur and fire, and the other women come out with torches and embrace him.

23.1.title: Eurycleia wakes Penelope
23.1.text: Eurycleia hurries to the upper room and wakes Penelope with the news that Odysseus is home and has killed the suitors. Penelope thinks the gods have driven the old nurse mad. Eurycleia tells her that the beggar was Odysseus, that the dead lie heaped at the courtyard gates, and that she saw the old scar herself when she washed his feet. Penelope still believes some god has killed the suitors, but she agrees to go down and see.

23.2.title: Penelope sits in silence
23.2.text: Penelope comes down into the hall and sits by the far wall in the firelight, facing Odysseus; for a long time she says nothing. Telemachus reproaches her, and she answers that she and Odysseus have signs known only to the two of them. Odysseus smiles and turns to another care: they have killed the best young men of Ithaca. He has the bard play for dancing, so that people passing the house will think a wedding is being held.

23.3.title: The test of the bed
23.3.text: The housekeeper Eurynome bathes and dresses Odysseus, and Athena makes him taller and more handsome. He sits down again facing Penelope, calls her heart hard and asks the nurse to make up a bed for him alone. To test him, Penelope tells Eurycleia to move his own bed out of the bedroom he built. Odysseus flares up: no man could move that bed, for he built the room round a living olive tree and shaped its trunk into the bedpost.

23.4.title: Penelope knows her husband
23.4.text: Penelope's knees give way: only the two of them and one maid know the secret of the bed. She runs to Odysseus in tears, throws her arms round his neck and asks him not to be angry that she feared for so long to be deceived by a stranger. Odysseus weeps, holding his wife in his arms. Athena makes the night long and holds Dawn back by the stream of Ocean.

23.5.title: What Tiresias foretold
23.5.text: Odysseus tells Penelope that their trials are not over: in the house of Hades the soul of Tiresias foretold one more. He must go from town to town with an oar until he meets people who do not know the sea and take the oar for a winnowing fan; there he is to plant it and sacrifice to Poseidon. Then he may go home, where a gentle death will come to him in old age. Eurynome and the nurse make the bed, and husband and wife go to their room.

23.6.title: Odysseus retells his wanderings
23.6.text: In bed Penelope tells Odysseus what she endured from the suitors, and he tells her all his wanderings. He begins with the Cicones, the Lotus-eaters and the Cyclops, then Aeolus, the Laestrygonians, Circe and the house of Hades. He goes on to the Sirens, the Wandering Rocks, Charybdis and Scylla, the cattle of Helios and the loss of his ship and men. He ends with Calypso on Ogygia and the Phaeacians who sent him home, and then he falls asleep.

23.7.title: Odysseus leaves the town
23.7.text: When Odysseus has had his sleep, Athena lets Dawn rise from Ocean. He tells Penelope that he is going to the farm to see his father and that word of the killing will spread at sunrise: she is to stay in her upper room and see no one. He arms and wakes Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius, who arm as well. It is already light when the four leave the palace, but Athena hides them in darkness and leads them out of the town.

24.1.title: Hermes leads the souls away
24.1.text: Hermes calls the souls of the dead suitors out with his golden wand, and they follow him with thin cries. He leads them past the stream of Ocean, the gates of the Sun and the land of dreams to the meadow of asphodel, where the souls of the dead live. There they find the souls of Achilles, Patroclus, Antilochus and Ajax. The soul of Agamemnon comes up, and with it those who died with him in the house of Aegisthus.

24.2.title: Achilles and Agamemnon
24.2.text: The soul of Achilles tells Agamemnon that he should have died at Troy, where all the Achaeans would have raised him a tomb. Agamemnon answers that Achilles was the fortunate one. He tells how his mother Thetis came out of the sea and how gods and men mourned him for seventeen days. His bones lie with those of Patroclus in a golden jar under a great mound by the Hellespont; Agamemnon himself was killed on his return by Aegisthus and his own wife.

24.3.title: Amphimedon's story
24.3.text: Hermes comes up with the souls of the suitors, and Agamemnon recognises Amphimedon, once his host on Ithaca, and asks how they all died. Amphimedon tells how Penelope put them off for three years by weaving a shroud for Laertes and unpicking it at night. Then Odysseus came home as a beggar, strung the bow and killed them all with Telemachus; their bodies still lie unburied. Agamemnon calls Odysseus fortunate in his wife and says the gods will make a song for Penelope.

24.4.title: Odysseus finds his father
24.4.text: Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus and Philoetius come down from the town to the farm of Laertes. Odysseus sends the others into the house to prepare a meal and goes alone into the vineyard, where he finds his father in patched clothes, digging round a plant. He weeps under a pear tree, then decides to test him first. He praises the garden, asks the old man whose slave he is and whether this is Ithaca, and says he once had a guest from Ithaca, the son of Laertes.

24.5.title: The stranger from Alybas
24.5.text: Laertes weeps: this is Ithaca, he says, but his son must have died far from home. He asks the stranger who he is. Odysseus answers that he is Eperitus from Alybas, that a god drove him here from Sicania, and that this is the fifth year since Odysseus left Alybas. Laertes pours dust over his grey head; Odysseus springs to embrace him and tells him that he is his son and has killed the suitors.

24.6.title: The scar and the trees
24.6.text: Laertes asks for a sure sign. Odysseus shows him the scar from the boar on Parnassus and names the trees that Laertes gave him in this orchard when he was a child: thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, forty fig trees and fifty rows of vines. Laertes' knees give way, and he faints in his son's arms. When he comes to, he fears that the Ithacans will soon come against them; Odysseus tells him to take heart and come to the house.

24.7.title: The meal at the farm
24.7.text: Father and son go to the house, where Telemachus and the two herdsmen are carving meat and mixing wine. The old Sicel servant bathes Laertes, and Athena makes him taller and sturdier. Laertes wishes he had stood beside his son against the suitors as he was when he took Nericus, the town on the mainland shore. As they sit down to eat, old Dolius and his sons come in from the fields, recognise Odysseus and greet him.

24.8.title: The assembly of the Ithacans
24.8.text: Rumour of the suitors' death runs through the town. The families carry their dead out of the palace of Odysseus and bury them, send those from other towns home by ship, and gather in the assembly place. Eupeithes, father of Antinous, calls for revenge before Odysseus can escape to Pylos or Elis. Medon says he saw a god helping Odysseus, and Halitherses tells them the fault is their own, but more than half take up arms and follow Eupeithes.

24.9.title: Athena asks Zeus
24.9.text: On Olympus Athena asks Zeus whether he means to bring more war or to make peace between the two sides. Zeus answers that the revenge of Odysseus was her own plan and that she may do as she likes. But he says what would be right: now that Odysseus has had his revenge, let both sides swear an oath, let Odysseus be king for life, and let the gods make the families forget the killing. Athena darts down from the peaks of Olympus.

24.10.title: Peace on Ithaca
24.10.text: The Ithacans reach the farm, and the twelve men there arm and go out. Athena joins them in the shape of Mentor and has Laertes throw his spear, which kills Eupeithes. Odysseus and Telemachus fall on the front ranks, but Athena shouts to the Ithacans to stop; they drop their weapons and run for the town. When Odysseus rushes after them, Zeus casts a thunderbolt and Athena tells him to stop; she sets a sworn peace between the two sides.
